summary: Weekly POC sync focused on validating steady-state throughput and stability. SE shared initial 2-hour run results; customer asked for 24-hour steady-state with specific concurrency/latency targets. Discussed queueing/backpressure behavior, continuous batching knobs, and fallback routing. Agreed next steps and owners; scheduling follow-up to review extended run and update pilot pricing.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick roll call?
[00:07] Jordan (Cobalt): Hi Jordan here. Priya and Derek on as well. Ana's on too.
[00:12] Maya: Great, we wanted to run through the steady-state validation after the 2-hour run Ethan posted yesterday. Ethan, want to summarize?
[00:21] Ethan (Redwood SE): Yeah, sure. So we ran two configs: concurrency 8 and concurrency 16, both with continuous batching enabled and KV cache warm. The 2h run showed average token throughput per GPU of ~1.2M tokens/hour at 8c and ~1.9M at 16c but with slightly higher tail latency on the 16c run. There were a couple of micro-spikes when queue depth hit ~120 requests.
[00:45] Priya (Cobalt): When you say "continuous batching enabled" - is that the auto batch-size knob or the prefix caching? just want to be sure terminology aligns.
[00:55] Ethan: Good call. So continuous batching here means request coalescing in the runtime plus dynamic batch-size selection based on observed inter-arrival times. Not prefix cache; KV cache was warm which helped.
[01:07] Derek (Cobalt): we saw the 95th jump, is that due to batching delay or queueing backlog? we care about 95th < 300ms for our interactive UI.
[01:16] Ethan: It's a mix. At higher conc the runtime intentionally waits up to 20ms to assemble a larger batch which increases P95 slightly. But the big contributor in the spikes was queueing when downstream GPU kernels had momentary jitter — there's some queuing amplification.
[01:33] Jordan: can you explain queuing amplification? not sure I follow.
[01:37] Ethan: Sure. If kernel latency increases for a few iterations, the queue builds; because continuous batching increases batch size to catch up, that temporarily raises per-request latency further — a positive feedback loop. We can blunt that with adaptive max batch-delay or with concurrency caps.
[01:51] Maya: So two levers: reduce batch-delay (less grouping) to hit P95, or cap concurrency and accept lower throughput.
[01:58] Priya: Our priority is consistent UX — P95 under 300ms for core flows. peak throughput is secondary for now. So looks like we need to tune for tail latency.
[02:09] Ethan: Totally makes sense. For the next run I propose: concurrency=12, batch-delay cap 12ms, and enable burst-buffering offload for short spikes. Also we'll enable the runtime's queue-prioritization for user-facing routes.
[02:25] Ana (Cobalt): What's burst-buffering offload? we haven't seen that in the docs.
[02:30] Ethan: It's an internal mechanism where small spikes are temporarily buffered in a fast CPU queue and served by a warmed small-batch path — less efficient but lower tail latency for short spikes. We'll include a notes section in the logs.
[02:41] Derek: will that increase cost significantly? our CFO watches token-engine costs closely.
[02:45] Maya: there's a cost tradeoff — the offload uses more GPU cycles per effective token in spike windows, but the hit is small if spikes are rare. We'll show cost delta in the updated pilot pricing scenarios.
[02:56] Jordan: last run had one OOM-ish event? the node restarted briefly. anything to do with batch sizes?
[03:03] Ethan: That restart looked like a kernel hiccup that coincided with a model hot-path memory peak; we have mitigations — reduce max batch size and enable kernel-selection fallback to smaller-kernel path. Also add a quick mem headroom threshold to trigger soft-throttle before OOM.
[03:20] Priya: For our model, average prompt length is 110 tokens, but we have long-context flows up to 1,200 tokens. Did your runs include long-context requests?
[03:29] Ethan: The 2h run was synthetic using your sample trace with 10% long-context. We'll ask for a larger trace for the 24h to be representative.
[03:35] Jordan: I'll export the request trace later today.
[03:39] Maya: Perfect. On fallback routing: we discussed auto-fallback to a slightly quantized variant during sustained saturation. Ethan, any concerns about quality regression?
[03:47] Ethan: We did a quick eval on 100 prompts; the quantized variant had minor diff and some hallucination shifts in the long-context tests. We'll tag those prompts so Priya can run her eval suite. We can also do canary percentages — e.g., start 5% fallbacks during non-peak.
[04:05] Priya: Please do the tagged set. I want to measure Rouge/EM style metrics against our golden set.
[04:10] Ethan: We'll push the flagged set with metrics.
[04:13] Samir (CSM): small note on logs: can you include per-request routing metadata and kernel id so we can trace tail events?
[04:20] Ethan: yes we'll enable debug-level trace for the 24h run and upload compressed logs.
[04:24] [05:00] (short silence / file share)
[05:05] Jordan: also thinking about concurrency targets per region — US East traffic is heavier. Could we do region routing and small capacity bump for east?
[05:14] Maya: yes we can route by policy and put reserve capacity in us-east. That would reduce cross-region latency and reduce queuing. We'll include dedicated small reserve in pricing options.
[05:23] Derek: on security — we need confirmation on KMS usage for model artifacts and token logs. Are audit logs preserved in Private?
[05:30] Maya: For Private deployments, audit logs are customer-facing and can be pushed to your SIEM. For Hosted pilot we provide encrypted-at-rest with customer-managed KMS as an add-on. We'll send the security doc.
[05:42] Priya: Does the debug trace include any PII? we scrub tokens and prompts right?
[05:46] Ethan: By default we obfuscate user identifiers and redact known PII. If you need additional scrubbing we can do a pipeline before sharing.
[05:54] Jordan: timeline question — we need pilot acceptance criteria by next week. What minimal metrics should we target?
[06:01] Maya: Suggested acceptance: sustained 24h run with P95 < 300ms for core flows, throughput within 85% of target, and no more than one soft-restart event. Also validate fallback quality on tagged prompts. Thoughts?
[06:12] Ana: that seems reasonable. We'll add cost per 1M tokens delta threshold.
[06:17] Maya: Good. Ethan, can you confirm the instrumentation we'll include in the run artifacts?
[06:21] Ethan: Perf.csv with per-minute token counts, per-minute P50/P95/P99, queue-depth histogram, kernel-id traces, and routing decisions. Also compressed latency flame for the jitter window.
[06:33] Priya: Will the perf.csv include request-level IDs so we can map to our trace?
[06:37] Ethan: yes, we'll include request hashes (non-PII) so you can correlate.
[06:41] [10:00] (discussion about test harness specifics, minor crosstalk)
[10:22] Derek: about the autoscaler — in the last spike we saw delayed scale up. is that because scale is conservative?
[10:28] Ethan: Our autoscaler has a conservative cool-down to avoid thrashing; for pilots we can reduce cool-down and add faster burst capacity. The tradeoff is transient cost.
[10:38] Jordan: what's the faster burst? like 30s?
[10:40] Ethan: We can have 60s cold-start for a new micro-pool, and a pre-warmed buffer pool that gives near-instant capacity but costs more. For the 24h run we can keep a small pre-warm buffer to avoid scale-up latency.
[10:51] Maya: That pre-warm buffer will be in the pricing scenarios.
[10:55] Priya: One more question: for quantized fallback quality, can we limit fallback to short-context only? long-context is sensitive.
[11:02] Ethan: Absolutely. We'll restrict auto-fallback to requests under 512 tokens by default and make it configurable.
[11:07] Jordan: great. Anything else on tuning knobs?
[11:11] Ethan: We'll also run an experiment with soft-throttling where the runtime rejects low-priority background requests once queue depth crosses threshold — that should keep P95 for interactive flows.
[11:22] Ana: That would help. We'll identify background vs interactive routes in the next day.
[11:27] Maya: Ok to recap: Redwood runs a 24-hour steady-state with conc=12, batch-delay cap 12ms, pre-warm buffer enabled, fallback rules limited to <512 tokens. We'll include debug traces, perf.csv, and cost delta. Cobalt provides production trace and acceptance thresholds. Follow-up on 2026-06-05.
[11:44] Jordan: yep. Also can you add a section in the results about correlation between request size distribution and queue depth? That really helps our infra team.
[11:53] Ethan: noted. We'll surface that in the report.
[11:58] Priya: and please tag the golden prompt set so I can run automated QA.
[12:02] Samir: I'll send meeting invite for the June 5th result review, 60 minutes.
[12:06] Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the pricing sheet and security doc.
[12:10] Jordan: thanks. bye.
[12:12] (meeting ends)

Notes and imperfections: occasional speaker mislabels for one minute early in the call; transcription mangled "KV" as "K-V" in places; some timestamps approximate. Logs referenced: /redwood/pilot/cobalt/run-2026-05-28-2h.tar.gz (uploaded), next run path will be /redwood/pilot/cobalt/run-2026-05-29-24h.tar.gz when ready.
